preview: An interview experience at BNY for an internship role detailing the online assessment, technical round, and HR round with a stipend of 75,000/month.
content: Interview Experience BNY MELLON Stipend:75,000/month ADWAITA PATANE B.Tech Electronics Engineering Procedure 1. Online Assessment(OA) 2. Offline PPT 3. Offline Technical Round 4. Offline HR Round Online Assessment The OA consisted of 4 DSA questions which were to be completed within 2 hours. The questions were as follows: 1. Redundancy Maximizer We have been given a binary string servers where: '1' means a server is working. '0' means a server is redundant (backup). We want to find the number of distinct possible counts of working servers after optimally flipping a contiguous segment of servers (i.e., changing '0' → '1' or '1' → '0'). Example 1 Input: servers = "1100" Original working servers = 2. Flip "0" → "1" → 3 working servers. Flip "00" → "11" → 4 working servers. Flip "1" → "0" → 1 working server. Possible counts = {1, 2, 3, 4} → Answer = 4 Example 2 Input: servers = "111" Original working = 3. Flipping any subarray decreases count. Possible counts = {1, 2, 3} → Answer = 3 Approach what I did was, I kind of treated this like Kadane’s algorithm (the max subarray sum thing). I thought of every '0' as a +1 (since flipping it gives me one more working server) and every '1' as a -1 (since flipping it means I lose one working server). Then I just looked for the subarray that gives me the biggest gain, and also the one that gives me the biggest loss. Once I had those, I just added them to the original count of working servers to figure out the minimum and maximum I could possibly get. Finally, the answer is just the range of values from that minimum to that maximum. 2. Optimal Team Size We are given n players. For each player, we have: lowerSkill[i]: minimum skill position they can play. higherSkill[i]: maximum skill position they can play. We want to find the largest possible team size we can form, such that for each position from 0 to teamSize-1, some player can fit there (within their skill range). Example 1 Input: lowerSkill = [0, 1, 2] higherSkill = [2, 2, 2] We can form team of size 3 because: Player 1 fits position 0 Player 2 fits position 1 Player 3 fits position 2 Answer = 3 Example 2 Input: lowerSkill = [0, 0, 1] higherSkill = [1, 2, 2] Max possible team size = 2 (cannot place 3 players because constraints won’t match) Answer = 2 Approach just used Binary Search on the possible team size. For each mid value, I checked if it’s actually possible to form a team of that size using a greedy method (I called it canFormTeam). If it worked, then I moved the search to the right (trying for a bigger team). If it didn’t work, I moved left (settling for a smaller team). 3. Cluster Sizes (DSU / Union-Find) Given are a list of integers serverProp. Each number represents a server property (like an ID). Two servers belong to the same cluster if they share any factor greater than 1. Find the size of the cluster each server belongs to. Example 1 Input: serverProp = [5, 10, 15, 20] 10 shares factor 5 with 5. 15 shares factor 5 with 5. 20 shares factor 10 with 10. All are connected. Output = [4, 4, 4, 4] Example 2 Input: serverProp = [7, 11, 13] All are prime, no shared factors. Each cluster size = 1. Output = [1, 1, 1] Approach Use Disjoint Set Union (DSU).For each number, union it with all its factors.After union, count cluster sizes by root.Output cluster size for each element. 4. High Priority Subset We are given n intervals with: start[i]: start time of a task. finish[i]: finish time of a task. We want to find the maximum size of a subset of intervals such that all of them overlap with at least one common task. Example 1 Input: start = [1, 2, 3, 4] finish = [2, 3, 5, 5] Task 3 ([3,5]) overlaps with tasks 2 ([2,3]) and 4 ([4,5]). Max overlapping subset = {2,3,4} size 3. Answer = 3 Example 2 Input: start = [1, 5, 9] finish = [4, 8, 12] No three overlap at once. Max subset size = 1. Answer = 1 Approach For each interval, check how many other intervals overlap with it Take maximum overlap count. I had solved All the testcases for the medium-hard and easy problems and 14/15 for the two medium problems so I was pretty confident about my chances of getting shortlisted for the interview and called my seniors to ask how to prepare for it. The shortlisted candidates were to be announced after the offline ppt which was more than a week later so I utilized this time to go over my projects and create a STAR method introduction on them and revised the core topics like OS DBMS OOPS. Offline Pre-Placement Talk After the Online Assessment (OA), a Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) is usually held for all applicants. It's important to attend the PPT because it provides crucial information about the company ,such as work culture, values and locations. This information might be asked later in the HR interviews to check you attentiveness. The PPT also helps you come up with thoughtful questions for the interviewers, which is essential when they ask, "Do you have any questions for us?" You should always have a couple of good questions ready for this. The shortlisted students were announced after the PPT. The first round was purely technical for me and the second round was taken by a senior person. Round 1:Technical Interview The interviews had started right after the PPT at around 12:30 pm, but my first interview didn’t begin until 3:30. I entered the room with a smile, even though I was in shambles inside from pacing around, watching others come out of their interviews with mixed emotions, going for lunch while I didn’t even know when mine would start. Still, I walked in confidently and greeted the interviewer with, “Hello! Good Afternoon.” He greeted me back, introduced himself, and began with the classic: “Tell me about yourself.” Now, this is where it’s really important to have a good introduction ready. Even though I hadn’t won many hackathons or anything, he was still very impressed with my introduction and even chatted a bit about what I had mentioned in it. Then, for some reason, while others were being asked only 1–2 DSA questions, my interviewer asked me quite a lot of them. He covered different sorting techniques, asked me to write pseudocode for merge sort and quick sort, reverse a linked list, solve N-Queens, Valid Parentheses, traversals on trees, DFS, BFS, and even converting infix to postfix. These are just some of the questions I remember. Honestly, if you just get your fundamentals correct, this part becomes a lot easier. After that, he asked me about PSQL since I had mentioned quite a few data-structure-heavy projects. We had a nice discussion on those. Then he moved on to OOP and asked me to explain the four pillars of OOPS, which I did with examples. He also asked why I preferred Java as my main language and brought up some topics in Java I wasn’t too familiar with. I was honest and said I didn’t know much about those topics. He appreciated that and said, “Let it go, you’ve done very well till now.” Then he told me I could leave. The interview lasted around 40 minutes. One tip: Always explain your thought process aloud so the interviewer can follow your approach. And always mention the space and time complexities, even if they don’t specifically ask for them. Round 2:HR Round The HR round was fairly quick—it was mostly resume and project-based discussion. Although the interviewer cross-questioned many of my answers, I stayed confident in them, remained calm and composed, and answered to the best of my abilities. He first asked me to explain my project and then went deeper into the technologies I had mentioned in it. Since he was also a big data enthusiast, we had quite a lot to talk about. This round lasted only about 25 minutes, as it was getting pretty late and the interviews needed to be wrapped up. At one point, he asked me for an example of regression—one of the easiest topics. I gave him a few, but he wanted it framed in another way. By then, it was around 7 o’clock, and I was very tired since I hadn’t eaten anything all day. Still, I tried answering as best as I could. Despite feeling tired and very over it, I made sure not to show it in my body language. I calmly responded, “Right now, I can’t think of more, but if I remember any, I will let you know.” It seemed like he was testing how I handled pressure and cross-questioning. By the end of it, he seemed overall very happy with me. Result The result of shortlisted students was announced on the same day. Preparation 1. Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA): Solve most questions from Striver’s A2Z sheet, which covers important standard problems across all topics. 2. Database Management Systems (DBMS) & Operating Systems (OS): Focus on understanding the key concepts in the syllabus. I had done it from an apna college pdf and gate samshers for DBMS 3. Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): Refer to articles on GeeksforGeeks and practice writing code for each OOP concept. 4. Projects: Be well-versed in your projects and use the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) method to explain your role and contributions, especially for team projects. 5. Resume: Know your resume thoroughly and anticipate questions related to your project tech stack (e.g., Firebase, MongoDB, React) using resources like InterviewBit or GeeksforGeeks. 6. CS Fundamentals: Revise core concepts in Operating Systems, OOP, and DBMS. If time permits, also review Computer Networks (CN) and low/high-level design concepts. 7. Additional Resources: Seek help from seniors for resume reviews and mock interviews. 8. Dressing for Interviews: Dress appropriately for in-person interviews, as a professional appearance is crucial.
